blocks.md: **A linked list is a chain of boxes; each box holds a value and a NOTE telling where the next box lives. You must start at the HEAD and follow notes.**

steps: Boxes may live ANYWHERE in memory — arrows glue them into order
Lost the head pointer = lost the whole list

blocks.label: the node — memorize forever
blocks.py:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.next = None            # born pointing nowhere

head = Node(10)
head.next = Node(20)
head.next.next = Node(30)           # chain built inline

sections.title: The walks & rewires you own today

blocks.label: traversal — THE loop
blocks.py:
temp = head                         # never lose head!
while temp:
    print(temp.val, end=' ')
    temp = temp.next                # hop along the note

blocks.label: insert at head — one rewire
blocks.py:
node = Node(5)
node.next = head                    # point at OLD first
head = node                         # crown new king
# order matters - head=node first would orphan the list

blocks.label: delete a node by value — dodge around it
blocks.py:
prev.next = target.next             # crowd steps over the hole
# Python GC reclaims target automatically (no delete needed)

blocks.md: **Golden rules:** (1) keep a `temp` walker, protect `head`. (2) Rewire BEFORE delete. (3) Every `new` needs one `delete` someday — or smart pointers later.
**Insertion/deletion = pointer REWIRING, never shifting. That's the entire superpower of lists.**

blocks.label: reverse — the rite of passage (guided)
blocks.py:
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    ahead = cur.next                 # save next BEFORE cutting
    cur.next = prev                  # flip arrow backward
    prev, cur = cur, ahead           # step both forward
head = prev                          # old tail is new head

options: cur->next gets overwritten — without saving, rest of list lost

items.q: Length counting uses which loop shape?

items.title: Construct from Array + Print
hints: Keep tail pointer while building to avoid n² head-inserts.

solutionCode.label: keep a tail pointer so appending stays O(1)

items.complexity: Build O(n) with a tail pointer. Naive head-append without a tail is O(n^2). Space O(n) for the nodes.

followups.q: Why does appending without a tail pointer cost O(n^2)?
followups.a: Each append walks from the head to find the end — 1 + 2 + ... + n steps, which is n(n+1)/2. Keeping the tail makes every append O(1), so building is O(n). It is the single most common performance bug in list construction.

followups.q: What does the dummy node buy?
followups.a: It removes the special case for the first insertion. Without it every append needs "if head is null, set head, else append to tail". With it, tail always points at a real node, so one line handles both. The dummy is discarded by returning dummy.next.

solutionCode.label: walk and count
solutionCode.py:
def length_iterative(head) -> int:
    count = 0
    t = head
    while t:
        count += 1
        t = t.next
    return count

followups.q: Why walk with a temporary rather than advancing head itself?
followups.a: Advancing head destroys the caller's only reference to the list — the nodes become unreachable and, in C++, leak. In Python the list survives because the caller holds its own reference, but the function still cannot walk it twice. Never move the parameter you were handed.

followups.q: What happens on a cyclic list?
followups.a: It loops forever. Length is only defined for a null-terminated list; if cycles are possible you need Floyd's detection first. Worth naming as a precondition rather than assuming it.

items.title: Length (recursive)
hints: 'I solve one part, recursion handles rest' debut.

solutionCode.label: one node plus whatever recursion returns

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the call stack — this is the cost recursion adds over the loop.

followups.q: State the mantra.
followups.a: "I solve one part; recursion handles the rest." This function counts exactly one node — its own — and trusts the recursive call to return the length of everything after it. You never trace the whole stack; you verify the base case and the one-step reduction.

followups.q: Why is the recursive version worse here?
followups.a: It costs O(n) stack space where the loop costs O(1), and at n = 10^5 it blows the default stack in both C++ and Python. Recursion earns its keep on branching structures like trees; on a linear walk it is strictly a downgrade.

items.title: Search Key

solutionCode.label: walk while counting the 1-indexed position

items.complexity: Time O(n) worst case, space O(1).

followups.q: Why can a linked list not be binary searched?
followups.a: Binary search needs O(1) access to the middle element. Reaching index n/2 in a list costs n/2 steps, so each "halving" is linear and the total becomes O(n) anyway — with worse constants than a plain scan. Random access is the property arrays have and lists do not.

followups.q: Why 1-indexed here when arrays are 0-indexed?
followups.a: Because the problem says so — position 1 is the head. Mixing conventions between the position returned and the loop counter is the bug to watch for. Decide the convention up front and make the initialiser match it.

items.title: Insert at Position K
items.statement: Insert value before k-th node (1-indexed); handle head case.
hints: newNode->next = prev->next FIRST, then prev->next = newNode.

solutionCode.label: wire the new node forward BEFORE relinking the predecessor
solutionCode.py:
def insert_at_position(head, k: int, val: int):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)        # dummy makes the head case ordinary
    prev = dummy
    i = 1
    while i < k and prev.next:
        prev = prev.next
        i += 1
    node = ListNode(val)
    node.next = prev.next            # FIRST: do not lose the tail
    prev.next = node                 # THEN: splice it in
    return dummy.next

followups.q: What breaks if you reverse the two assignments?
followups.a: Setting prev.next = node first overwrites the only pointer to the rest of the list, so node.next = prev.next then points at node itself — a self-loop, and everything after it is leaked. The order is not stylistic; it is the difference between a working list and a corrupted one.

followups.q: Why a dummy rather than an if for k == 1?
followups.a: Inserting before the head is the only case where there is no predecessor to modify. A dummy manufactures one, so the same two lines handle head insertion and interior insertion. It also means the function returns dummy.next, which is correct whether or not the head changed.

solutionCode.label: dummy again, then bypass and free
solutionCode.py:
def delete_at_position(head, k: int):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    i = 1
    while i < k and prev.next:
        prev = prev.next
        i += 1
    if prev.next is None:
        return dummy.next            # k out of range: nothing to remove
    prev.next = prev.next.next       # bypass; Python's GC reclaims the node
    return dummy.next

followups.q: Why bypass before deleting?
followups.a: Reading target->next after delete is a use-after-free — the memory may already be reused and the pointer is garbage. Save what you need, rewire, then free. In Python the GC hides this, which is exactly why it is worth naming when writing the C++ version.

followups.q: Why does deleting the head need no special case here?
followups.a: Because prev starts at the dummy, so "delete the first node" is just prev->next = target->next with prev being the dummy. Returning dummy.next then picks up the new head automatically. Without the dummy this needs its own branch.

items.title: Reverse Iterative
items.statement: Section-guided reverse; then WITHOUT looking at notes.

solutionCode.label: save ahead, flip, double-step
solutionCode.py:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        ahead = cur.next     # SAVE: the flip is about to destroy this
        cur.next = prev      # FLIP
        prev = cur           # DOUBLE-STEP both pointers forward
        cur = ahead
    return prev              # cur is None; prev is the new head

followups.q: Why return prev rather than cur?
followups.a: The loop ends when cur becomes null — it has walked off the end. prev is sitting on the last node visited, which after the flips is the new head. Returning cur returns null and silently loses the entire list.

followups.q: Why must ahead be saved before the flip?
followups.a: cur->next = prev overwrites the only pointer to the rest of the list. Without the save, the next iteration has nowhere to go and the remaining nodes are orphaned. Three pointers is the minimum: where you came from, where you are, where you are going.

solutionCode.label: accumulate in a wide type
solutionCode.py:
def sum_of_nodes(head) -> int:
    total = 0
    t = head
    while t:
        total += t.val
        t = t.next
    return total

followups.q: Why a 64-bit accumulator?
followups.a: With 10^5 nodes holding values near 10^9, the total reaches 10^14 — well past the 2.1x10^9 int ceiling. The individual values fit in int; the sum does not. Mismatched accumulator width is a silent wrong answer, not a crash.

followups.q: Does Python need the same care?
followups.a: No — Python integers are arbitrary precision, so the sum simply grows. That difference is worth stating explicitly when you present both languages, because it is a real semantic gap rather than a syntax one.

items.title: Print Reverse (recursion warmup)
items.statement: Print list backwards WITHOUT reversing structure.
hints: Recurse to end first; print AFTER recursive call returns.

solutionCode.label: recurse to the end first, print on the way back up

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the call stack.

followups.q: Why does printing after the recursive call reverse the order?
followups.a: The recursion descends to the tail before any output happens. As each frame returns, it prints its own node — so the deepest frame (the tail) prints first and the shallowest (the head) prints last. The call stack is acting as an implicit stack data structure.

followups.q: How is this different from actually reversing the list?
followups.a: The pointers are never touched — the structure is identical afterwards. That is the point of the exercise: you can traverse backwards without mutating, at the cost of O(n) stack. Reversing is O(1) space but destructive unless you reverse back.

items.title: Doubly: Insert Front & Back
items.statement: Maintain head+tail DLL; insert both ends; print forward and backward.
hints: Every insert sets BOTH next and prev.

solutionCode.label: every insertion writes BOTH directions

items.complexity: O(1) per insertion at either end. Space O(n).

followups.q: What is the failure mode of forgetting one direction?
followups.a: The forward walk looks perfect and the backward walk silently truncates or loops. A DLL has two independent invariants — node.next.prev == node and node.prev.next == node — and only the backward traversal tests the second. Always print both directions when debugging.

followups.q: Why does the empty case set head and tail to the same node?
followups.a: A one-element deque has that element at both ends. Setting only head leaves tail null, so the next push_back allocates a second head and the list forks. The empty branch is the only place the two pointers are assigned together, which is why it needs its own line.
